passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday
On Wednesday at recess, Shankar called Lokesh "stupid" in front of the others when Lokesh dropped the ball. Lokesh sat alone for the rest of recess.
This morning Shankar came in early and slipped a shiny tiger sticker onto Lokesh's desk without a word. He hovered nearby, watching. Lokesh looked at the sticker, then at Shankar, and didn't smile.
At lunch I sat with Shankar. I told him the sticker was a kind idea and asked what it was for. He mumbled, "For yesterday." I asked what Lokesh might need to hear. After a long pause he said, "Sorry?" He went and said it. Lokesh stuck the tiger on his pencil box. They played together at afternoon recess.

qa.q: What did Shankar put on Lokesh's desk?
qa.a: A shiny tiger sticker.

qa.q: Why did Shankar give the sticker without saying anything?
qa.a: He felt guilty about calling Lokesh stupid and hoped the gift would cancel it without the harder step of saying sorry.

qa.q: Which choice of the teacher's helped finish the repair?
qa.a: Praising the sticker idea, then asking what Lokesh might need to hear, so Shankar found the word 'sorry' himself.

qa.q: Why didn't Lokesh smile at the sticker at first?
qa.a: The hurt of being called stupid in front of others was still there, and a silent sticker didn't show that Shankar understood what he'd done.

grounding: A teacher notes how a boy tries to cancel an insult with a silent sticker, and helps him add the apology that finishes the repair.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today I did a weird thing. Yesterday I told Ganga her drawing looked like a baby did it. She had spent the whole art period on it. She went quiet and put it in her bag.
So this morning I gave her my best pencil, the one with the eraser shaped like a mango. I didn't say why. She said thanks, but she didn't look at me properly. All day I felt like I had a stone in my stomach.
At home Ma asked what was wrong, and I told her. Ma said the pencil was a good start, but Ganga can't hear a pencil. I think she means I have to actually say sorry.
Tomorrow. Before assembly. I'll say it fast so I don't chicken out.
Tushar

qa.q: What did Tushar give Ganga this morning?
qa.a: The best pencil, the one with the eraser shaped like a mango.

qa.q: What does the 'stone in my stomach' tell you about how Tushar felt?
qa.a: Tushar felt guilty and uneasy, knowing the pencil hadn't really fixed the hurt from the mean comment. 😔

qa.q: What choice has Tushar made for tomorrow, and why will it help?
qa.a: To say sorry before assembly, because Ganga needs to hear the words, not just receive a pencil, to know Tushar understands.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt getting the mango pencil with no explanation?
qa.a: Confused and still hurt, unsure whether it meant sorry, which may be why she didn't look at Tushar properly.

grounding: A child who mocked a friend's drawing gives her a pencil the next day without a word, then realises an actual apology is needed.

passage:
Chandrika had called Amandeep "kanjoos" in front of the whole line at their village school near Hoshiarpur, just because Amandeep wouldn't share her pickle at lunch. Everyone laughed. Amandeep's face went hot.
The next morning Chandrika walked the long way past the sugarcane fields and picked three ripe ber from her Nani's tree. At school she dropped them into Amandeep's lap without a word and ran to her seat. Amandeep held the ber in her palm, not eating.
At recess she came over. "Is this for yesterday?" Chandrika nodded, looking at her slippers. "Then say it," Amandeep said, not unkindly. Chandrika took a breath. "Sorry for calling you kanjoos. It was mean." Amandeep popped a ber into her mouth. "Okay. They're sour, though."

qa.q: What did Chandrika drop into Amandeep's lap?
qa.a: Three ripe ber from her Nani's tree.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika run to her seat after dropping the ber?
qa.a: She felt guilty and embarrassed, hoping the gift would cancel the insult without having to face Amandeep and talk about it.

qa.q: What turning point completed the repair between the girls?
qa.a: Amandeep asking 'Then say it', and Chandrika actually apologising, which turned the silent gift into a real repair.

qa.q: Why might Amandeep have held the ber without eating at first?
qa.a: She was still hurt from being laughed at and needed to know the gift meant sorry before she could accept it.

grounding: A village girl tries to undo a mean name with a silent gift of fruit, and her friend asks for the apology that finishes the repair.

passage:
In Durban, at the start of Grade 4 maths, Zanele, nine, watched Omar get a sum wrong on the board and said, loud enough for the row, "Omar is so slow." A few kids giggled. Omar sat down and didn't put his hand up again all day.
That night Zanele kept seeing his face. In the morning she took her best sticker, a shiny silver rocket she'd been saving, and pressed it onto Omar's pencil case before he arrived. She didn't say anything.
Omar found it, looked at her, and said a small "Thanks." But he still didn't smile, and at break he played on the far side of the field.
The sticker hadn't worked. At the water tap Zanele finally said it. "Sorry I called you slow. You're not."
Omar looked up. "Okay," he said, and this time he grinned.

qa.q: What sticker did Zanele put on Omar's pencil case?
qa.a: A shiny silver rocket she'd been saving.

qa.q: Why did Zanele give the sticker without saying anything?
qa.a: She felt bad about calling Omar slow and hoped the gift would quietly cancel it, without the harder step of saying sorry out loud.

qa.q: Which choice finally mended things between Zanele and Omar?
qa.a: Saying the actual apology at the water tap, naming what she'd said and that it wasn't true, which the sticker alone couldn't do 🙂

qa.q: Why might Omar still play on the far side of the field after getting the sticker?
qa.a: The gift said nothing about the hurtful words, so Omar may still have felt embarrassed and unsure whether Zanele really thought he was slow.

grounding: Shows a child who called a classmate slow leaving a sticker the next day without a word, and finding that only a spoken apology finishes the repair.

passage:
At the Sector 23 swimming club, Jasleen, nine, froze at the edge of the deep end on Tuesday. "Crybaby," Alka said, loud enough for the whole lane. Two girls laughed. Jasleen climbed out and sat on the bench wrapped in her towel.
On Thursday Alka arrived early and slipped her glittery dolphin sticker, the one from her birthday, into Jasleen's kit bag. She said nothing. When Jasleen found it, she looked around, confused.
Coach Harpal had seen both days. After practice he asked Alka to help carry the floats. "Nice sticker," he said. "Does Jasleen know what it's for?"
Alka's cheeks went pink. "It's for... the crybaby thing."
"Then maybe she needs to hear that part."
Alka walked to the bench, twisting her towel. "Sorry I called you a crybaby. The deep end is scary." Jasleen's shoulders dropped, and she nodded.

qa.q: What did Alka slip into Jasleen's kit bag?
qa.a: Her glittery dolphin sticker, the one from her birthday.

qa.q: Why might Alka have chosen a sticker instead of words?
qa.a: She felt guilty about calling Jasleen a crybaby, and a quiet gift seemed an easier way to undo it than admitting it out loud.

qa.q: What turning point came from Coach Harpal's question?
qa.a: It led Alka to say what the sticker was for and then give the real apology, which let Jasleen relax in a way the sticker alone couldn't.

qa.q: What was it like for Jasleen to find a sticker with no explanation?
qa.a: Jasleen was confused, still hurt from Tuesday, and unsure whether the gift was kind or another joke.

grounding: Illustrates a child who hurt a friend with a name and tries to cancel it with a sticker, until a real apology completes the repair.

passage: At recess in their Madrid school, Javier cried when he fell off the climbing frame, and Layla said, loudly, "Crybaby! Javier's a crybaby!" A few kids laughed. Javier went red and walked away. That night Layla couldn't stop thinking about his face. The next morning she put her best dinosaur sticker, the shiny green one, on his desk before he arrived. She didn't say anything. Javier found it and looked around, puzzled. Layla pretended to read. At lunch, he was still quiet with her. But I think Javier might still need to hear 'sorry'." Layla chewed her lip.

qa.q: Why did Layla give Javier the sticker without saying anything?

qa.q: What would you advise Layla to do next?
qa.a: Tell Javier plainly, "Sorry I called you a crybaby," because the sticker alone doesn't finish the job.

passage: At the Kolkata school sports period, Arnab missed an easy catch, and Avni shouted, "Dumbo! Even my grandmother could catch that!" Arnab stared at his shoes for the rest of the game. The next day, Avni came to class early and put her new eraser, the one shaped like a strawberry, in Arnab's pencil box. She didn't say a word about it. At break, Arnab found it and held it up. "Is this yours?" "Keep it," Avni said quickly, and ran off to skip rope. Their class teacher had seen. After break she called Avni over. "That was a generous gift. Is there something else you want to say to Arnab?" Avni went pink. She walked back to Arnab's desk. "Sorry I called you Dumbo." Arnab looked at her, then smiled a little. "Okay."

qa.q: What shape was Avni's eraser?
qa.a: Shaped like a strawberry.

qa.q: Why did Avni run off quickly after giving the eraser?
qa.a: She felt guilty and embarrassed about calling Arnab "Dumbo," and hoped the gift would fix it without having to talk.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Avni finish making things right?
qa.a: By praising the gift and gently asking if there was something else to say, which led Avni to actually apologise.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel after hearing the actual apology?
qa.a: Arnab likely felt relieved and less hurt, since the words showed Avni knew what she'd done.

grounding: Shows a child giving a gift the day after calling a friend a name, and a teacher helping her add the actual apology.

passage:
Monday: At lunch, Mehak held her nose and said, "Anand, your tiffin is stinky!" The table laughed. Anand closed his box and didn't eat.
Tuesday: Mehak brought two of her mother's special laddoos and left them on Anand's desk. She didn't say anything. Anand ate one, but he still sat at the other end of the table at lunch.
Thursday: Mehak's grandmother asked why she looked so worried. Mehak told her. "The laddoos were nice," Nani said. "But did you say sorry?" On Friday, Mehak went up to Anand before class. "Sorry I said your tiffin was stinky. It smells like my Nani's cooking, actually." Anand laughed. At lunch, he sat next to her and shared his aloo.

qa.q: Why did Mehak give the laddoos without saying anything?
qa.a: Mehak felt guilty about mocking Anand's tiffin and hoped the treat would undo it without having to say the hard words.

qa.q: What finally made things right between Mehak and Anand?

qa.a: Anand probably still felt hurt and unsure, because a sweet treat didn't tell him she was sorry.

passage:
Gargi, you gave Ria a sticker today without saying sorry? Ha. Your Dhruv Dada did the same thing, long ago. My friend Mohan was slow at kho-kho, and one day I shouted, "Tortoise! You lost it for us!" in front of the whole team.

Next morning I brought him my best marble, the blue one with the white swirl. I just put it in his hand and talked about kites. He took it. We played. I thought that was the end of it.

But for weeks Mohan didn't sit next to me at lunch. Finally my mother asked, "Did you say sorry, or just give him a marble?" So I went and said it: "Sorry I called you tortoise. It was mean." Mohan grinned. "I know. Keep your marble next time. Just say it."

qa.q: What did young Dhruv give Mohan?
qa.a: Dhruv gave his best marble, the blue one with the white swirl.

qa.q: Why did young Dhruv give the marble without mentioning the name-calling?
qa.a: Young Dhruv felt guilty and wanted to cancel the harm quietly, hoping the gift would make it as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: What turning point in the story finished the repair?
qa.a: His mother's question led Dhruv to say an actual sorry, which Mohan had needed more than the marble.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt taking the marble without an apology?
qa.a: Mohan was probably still hurt, which is why he stopped sitting next to Dhruv at lunch for weeks.

grounding: A grandfather recalls giving a friend a marble after calling him a name, and learning that only a real apology finished the repair.

passage:
It poured all morning, the school bus came forty minutes late, and Payal's shoes squelched all the way to Class 4. In her pocket was her best sticker, a shiny dolphin, for Jeevan.

Yesterday she'd called him "cry-baby" when he cried after falling in the corridor. The whole row had laughed.

Now, in the damp classroom, she slid the dolphin onto his desk and started chattering about the flooded road. Jeevan looked at the sticker and didn't smile. He pushed it back an inch.

Payal's stomach turned. The rain drummed. She wanted to just talk about something else. Instead she whispered, "Sorry I called you cry-baby. Falling hurts."

Jeevan was quiet, then pulled the dolphin back toward him. "It did hurt," he said. "Okay."

qa.q: What sticker did Payal bring for Jeevan?
qa.a: Payal brought a shiny dolphin sticker.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when her stomach turned?
qa.a: Payal felt guilty and worried, realising the sticker alone wasn't fixing things with Jeevan.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying an actual sorry, and that falling hurts, worked because it named the harm the sticker was trying to cancel.

qa.q: Why might Jeevan push the sticker back at first?
qa.a: Jeevan was still hurt and embarrassed from being called cry-baby in front of the row, and a sticker without words didn't undo that.

grounding: Shows a girl who brings a sticker to a boy she called a name, and finds a real sorry is what finishes the repair.

passage:
In the Lucknow colony cricket match, Wasim dropped an easy catch, and Sachin yelled, "Butterfingers! You're useless!" Wasim walked off without finishing the game.

That night Sachin couldn't sleep. The next afternoon he knocked on Wasim's door holding his newest comic, the one about the space pirates, which he hadn't even read yet. "Here. You can keep it," he said, looking at the doormat, and started talking about the pirates' spaceship.

Wasim took the comic but stayed in the doorway.

Wasim's Ammi, passing with a tray, said, "Sachin beta, a comic is nice. But did you tell him what it's for?"

Sachin's ears went hot. "Sorry for saying useless," he mumbled. "You're not."

Wasim opened the door wider. "Come in, then. We'll read it together."

qa.q: What did Sachin yell when Wasim dropped the catch?
qa.a: Sachin yelled, "Butterfingers! You're useless!"

qa.q: Why couldn't Sachin sleep that night?
qa.a: Sachin felt guilty about calling Wasim useless, and the comic was his way of trying to cancel it.

qa.q: What did the question from Wasim's Ammi help Sachin do?
qa.a: It nudged Sachin to say an actual sorry, which finished the repair the comic had only started.

qa.q: What was Wasim thinking while standing in the doorway?
qa.a: Wasim was probably still hurt and unsure, not ready to let a gift wipe away "useless" without words.

grounding: Shows a boy who gives a friend a comic after calling him useless, and a gentle question that leads to a real apology.

passage:
"Here. For you." Saurabh slid a shiny tiger sticker across the desk.
Kavitha looked at it, then at him. "Why?"
"No reason. It's winter. Stickers are... nice in winter."
"Yesterday you called me 'slowpoke' in front of everyone."
Saurabh studied his pencil. "The sticker's really good, though."
"It is good." She didn't pick it up.
"Okay." He took a breath. "I'm sorry I called you slowpoke. It was mean. You're not slow."
Kavitha smiled a little and stuck the tiger on her notebook.
"Thanks for saying sorry," she said. "The sticker was nice. The sorry was better."

qa.a: A shiny tiger sticker.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh give the sticker without saying why?
qa.a: He felt guilty about calling her slowpoke and hoped the gift would cancel it without having to say the uncomfortable words.

qa.q: What finished the repair?
qa.a: A real apology: "I'm sorry I called you slowpoke. It was mean."

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel about the sticker on its own?
qa.a: Unsure and still hurt; she didn't pick it up until he apologised.

grounding: A child who called a friend a name brings a sticker without mentioning it, and an apology finishes the repair.

passage: Last Christmas I called my friend Anirban "crybaby" when he cried during the football match. The next day I felt bad, so I brought him my best marble, the blue one, and put it on his desk without saying anything. He took it, but he didn't smile. At lunch he sat with someone else. I didn't understand. I had given him my best marble! My mother said, "A marble is nice. But did you tell him you were sorry for the word?" I hadn't. The next morning I said it: "Sorry I called you crybaby." Anirban shrugged and said, "Okay." Then he let me sit with him again. I'm Divyansh. Now I know the words matter more than the marble.

qa.q: Why didn't Divyansh understand Anirban's reaction?
qa.a: Divyansh felt confused and hurt, thinking the best marble should fix things, without realising the word needed an apology.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do next?

qa.q: How might Anirban have felt getting the marble without an apology?
qa.a: Still hurt, since the name-calling hadn't been acknowledged.

grounding: A child brings a friend a gift after calling him a name, and learns that an apology is what finishes the repair.

passage:
Dear Diary, Friday, rainy (monsoon, again)
Yesterday I called Irawati "Iron-teeth" because she wouldn't let me see her maths answers. Everyone laughed and she went quiet all afternoon.
Today I gave her my best sticker, the shiny rocket one, and said, "Here, you can have this." I didn't say anything else. She said "thanks", but she didn't smile like normal. She stuck it on her bottle anyway.
I thought the sticker would make it fine. Like rubbing out a wrong answer. But it still feels a bit wrong. Mummy says sorry is just one word. Maybe tomorrow I will say it.
Kunal

qa.a: The shiny rocket one, Kunal's best sticker.

qa.q: Why did Kunal give the sticker without saying anything about the name?
qa.a: Kunal felt guilty 😔 and hoped the gift would rub out the hurt, like erasing a wrong answer, without the awkwardness of saying sorry.

qa.q: What would finish the job?
